Explanation

When migrating an application that relies on the file system to Azure, it's important to consider the limitations of local storage in a cloud environment.
An application running inside a container could lose access to a file in local storage.

The following recommendations depend on the function of the file in local storage:

* Determine the storage needs for your application: Ephemeral storage or persistent storage. Ephemeral storage only persists until the cloud environment is restarted. Persistent storage is required for data that needs to persist across restarts.

* If persistent storage is needed, consider mounting Azure File Share or using Azure Blob Storage. Mount Azure file share allows your application to access files via the mount location. Azure blob storage is a scalable object store for data objects, such as text or binary files.

* Logging: Log to standard output and use Azure Monitor to collect and analyze the logs.

* Caching: Use Azure Managed Redis as a cache backing service.

* Configuration: Store configuration in Azure App Configuration instead of using the file system. Also store configuration settings in environment variables so that they can be updated without code changes.

Explanation

The application is using a Spring Boot version that has reached its End of OSS Support.
With the officially supported new versions from Spring, you can get the best experience. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose a supported Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and determine the most suitable supported Spring Boot version.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

3. Fix Compatibility Issues: Update deprecated code, replace removed features, and ensure dependencies are compatible with the new Spring Framework version.
4. Thoroughly Test: Run unit, integration, and end-to-end tests to make sure everything still works after the upgrade.

Architecture Diagram

This Java application is a multi-module assets manager that provides a Spring MVC web interface and an asynchronous worker for generating image thumbnails. It supports AWS S3 or local filesystem storage through profile-specific implementations.

Data Storage & External Services

PostgreSQL stores image metadata such as filename, content type, size, S3 key, and thumbnail key. AWS S3 is the production object store, while the dev profile uses a local filesystem directory. RabbitMQ provides the image-processing queue that decouples uploads from thumbnail generation.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Uses the StorageService interface with S3 and local filesystem implementations selected by Spring profiles.
  • Uses RabbitMQ and manual acknowledgments to decouple web uploads from asynchronous thumbnail processing.
  • Uses Spring Data JPA repositories for metadata while object data remains in S3 or the local filesystem.

DTOs & Contracts

ImageProcessingMessage is the asynchronous contract exchanged by the web and worker modules. It is a service-level mutable Lombok DTO with key, contentType, storageType, and size; Jackson serializes the RabbitMQ payload as JSON. S3StorageItem is a mutable Lombok view-model/response DTO used to render the storage list. ImageMetadata is the service-level JPA entity used for persistence metadata; it is owned by the web and worker modules and has its field details documented in data-architecture.md. There is no gateway aggregation DTO or OpenAPI/Swagger specification in the source. Protobuf and GraphQL schemas are not present.

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous: Browser-to-Thymeleaf HTTP calls are handled directly by Spring MVC. The web module calls local storage or AWS S3 synchronously and calls PostgreSQL through JPA in the S3 profile. There are no inter-service REST, gRPC, or gateway calls.
  • Asynchronous: Upload processing publishes ImageProcessingMessage to the durable RabbitMQ image-processing queue using RabbitTemplate.convertAndSend. The web module and worker module both listen on the queue; only the processor whose storageType matches its active implementation handles the work. BackupMessageProcessor is an optional profile-specific listener that acknowledges monitoring messages.
  • Storage profiles: dev selects local filesystem storage and LocalFileProcessingService; other profiles select AWS S3 and S3FileProcessingService.
  • Message acknowledgment: Processing success produces basicAck; worker processing failure produces basicNack(deliveryTag, false, false). Source comments describe routing to a dead-letter exchange/delayed retry, but no dead-letter exchange, retry queue, retry count, delay, timeout, or Redelivery configuration is explicitly declared.
  • Resilience: No circuit breaker, Resilience4j, Spring Retry, bulkhead, explicit HTTP timeout, client retry policy, or fallback is implemented. RabbitMQ uses manual acknowledgments; failed worker messages are rejected without requeue, with the intended retry behavior dependent on externally configured broker exchange bindings.
  • Discovery: No service-discovery client or API gateway is present. RabbitMQ and PostgreSQL use configured hostnames or defaults; no Eureka, Consul, Kubernetes DNS, or client-side load balancing is identified.
  • Startup: The web and worker services are independent Spring Boot applications that should be started after RabbitMQ and PostgreSQL/storage dependencies are available. No readiness probes or startup waits are configured in the modules.
  • Security: No authentication or authorization is implemented at the MVC API; the endpoints are publicly accessible and no role or permission checks are present. No HTTPS/TLS, OAuth2/JWT, Basic Auth, or Spring Security dependency is configured. RabbitMQ, database, and S3 credentials are externalized in properties, but HTTPS/S3/TLS behavior for the transport is not declared in application code.
  • Gateway aggregation: No API gateway or downstream service composition is present.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Local PostgreSQL container → starts before web and worker: scripts/startapp.sh starts assets-postgres; there is no Docker health check or wait-for-port mechanism.
  2. Local RabbitMQ container → starts before web and worker: scripts/startapp.sh starts assets-rabbitmq; there is no Docker health check or wait-for-port mechanism.
  3. Fixed 10-second delay → web and worker launch: startup proceeds after sleep 10; readiness is not verified.
  4. Web and worker start independently: both Maven Spring Boot processes launch in the background with dev; worker consumes the image-processing queue and web publishes or listens to it.

Azure deployment sequence:

  1. PostgreSQL, Storage, Service Bus, ACR, and Container Apps environment are provisioned.
  2. Managed identity and RBAC role assignments are created.
  3. Web and worker images are built and pushed to ACR.
  4. Web Container App is created, then PostgreSQL Service Connector adds passwordless datasource settings.
  5. Worker Container App is created after the web datasource values are retrieved.

No application readiness probes, actuator health endpoints, container health checks, startup timeout settings, or explicit ACA dependency conditions are declared.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

Local development uses Docker-provided PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ credentials. PostgreSQL is initialized with the database and credentials by scripts/startapp.sh or .cmd; RabbitMQ uses its management image defaults. AWS credentials remain in application properties when the non-dev profile is active and are not supplied as environment variables in the source scripts.

Azure deployment creates a user-assigned managed identity and assigns it Storage Blob Data Contributor, Azure Service Bus Data Owner, and ACR pull roles. The deployment also enables Microsoft Entra authentication on PostgreSQL and creates a Spring Boot Service Connector with the managed identity. The connector supplies datasource username and URL environment variables and enables passwordless Spring Cloud Azure credential settings. The storage account key is retrieved only during infrastructure setup to create the blob container and is not written to application properties.

No Key Vault, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Jasypt, DPAPI, or sealed-secrets mechanism is present.

Core Business Workflows

The application lets users store, browse, download, delete, and generate thumbnails for images across local filesystem or AWS S3 storage. It coordinates upload processing between a web application and a background worker through a durable message queue.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
ImageMetadataWeb and Worker / Asset MetadataRecords an uploaded asset and the lifecycle information for its original and thumbnail representations.References the original asset and optional thumbnail by storage key and URL.
ImageProcessingMessageWeb and Worker / Asynchronous Image ProcessingCarries the asset key and storage context needed for background thumbnail processing.References the original asset in ImageMetadata or storage.
S3StorageItemWeb / Asset CatalogPresentation view of an asset, including its name, size, timestamps, and access URL.Aggregates storage details with optional upload metadata.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
Assets Web ApplicationAsset management and catalogS3StorageItem, ImageMetadataSelected storage provider, PostgreSQL repository in non-development execution, RabbitMQ
LocalFileStorageServiceLocal asset storageS3StorageItemLocal filesystem; RabbitMQ
AwsS3ServiceCloud asset storageS3StorageItem, ImageMetadataAWS S3; PostgreSQL repository; RabbitMQ
Worker ApplicationImage processingImageProcessingMessage, ImageMetadataRabbitMQ; selected storage provider; PostgreSQL repository in S3 mode
RabbitMQ image-processing queueCross-context asynchronous processingImageProcessingMessageDurable queue with manual acknowledgments

The web application is the source of truth for upload initiation and asset metadata. Storage is the source of truth for asset bytes, while PostgreSQL is the source of truth for S3 upload metadata. The worker consumes storage-independent event data and updates S3 metadata after producing a thumbnail.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload and asynchronously process an image

The user submits a file through the asset upload page. The web controller rejects an empty file, otherwise the active storage service stores the original and publishes an image-processing message containing the key, content type, storage type, and size. The controller then confirms success or reports an I/O failure.

In S3 mode, the original is written to the configured bucket, metadata is persisted, and the queue receives the processing request. In development mode, the original is written to the local directory and the same queue receives the request. The worker validates that the message storage type matches its own provider; matching workers download the original, create a thumbnail, and store it back in the same provider. S3 mode also records the thumbnail key and URL in metadata.

Workflow 2: Browse and view assets

The user opens the asset list or selects an asset. The web application lists files from the active provider, enriches S3 entries with persisted upload timestamps when metadata exists, and prepares each item for viewing. Missing or unreadable asset states are handled as an empty list or an error response where appropriate.

Workflow 3: Delete an asset and its thumbnail

The user submits a deletion request. The active storage service deletes the original and attempts to delete the derived thumbnail. S3 mode removes matching metadata after deleting storage objects; local mode removes the matching thumbnail if present. The web application reports success or a failure message and returns to the asset catalog.

Other Workflows

Backup-profile processing can monitor image-processing messages and acknowledge or requeue them, but it does not modify asset storage or metadata.

Cross-Service Data Flows

The web application and worker exchange ImageProcessingMessage through the image-processing RabbitMQ queue. The web application publishes the storage key and provider type after the original file is saved. The worker filters by provider type, downloads the original through the same provider, generates the thumbnail, and uploads the derived image. In S3 mode, the worker cross-references metadata by original S3 key and updates thumbnail fields. RabbitMQ manual acknowledgments complete the flow only after processing succeeds or after the message is deliberately classified as a non-processing match.

If thumbnail processing fails, the worker rejects the message without requeueing it. The comment in the implementation indicates it is intended to be routed to a dead-letter exchange for delayed retry, subject to the external broker topology. If the processing message belongs to another storage provider, the worker acknowledges it without processing. There is no application-level fallback that recreates a missing thumbnail during viewing.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Business Rules

  • Uploading an empty multipart file is rejected; the user is redirected to the upload form with an error.
  • Upload paths prohibit directory traversal names containing .. in local mode.
  • Uploaded assets retain the original filename for display in local mode or receive a UUID-prefixed key in S3 mode.
  • Uploads are limited by multipart file and request settings of 10 MB each.
  • Thumbnail dimensions use a maximum of 600 pixels on the longest side while preserving aspect ratio; images already smaller than these dimensions are not enlarged.
  • JPEG thumbnails use 95 percent compression quality. PNG thumbnails use Deflate with zero compression quality for maximum fidelity.
  • A worker processes a message only when the message storage type matches the worker's configured provider.
  • Asset deletion removes both the original and the derived thumbnail when present.
  • S3 deletion removes matching persisted metadata after storage removal.
  • Local mode does not persist ImageMetadata; it derives catalog timestamps from filesystem attributes.

State and Processing Logic

  • A processing event begins as Pending by implication in RabbitMQ and becomes successfully acknowledged when the thumbnail is produced or the message is irrelevant to the provider.
  • A processing failure is represented by rejection without requeue, with the external broker responsible for delayed retry routing if dead-letter infrastructure is configured.
  • ImageMetadata sets upload and modification timestamps during JPA lifecycle callbacks.

Cross-Cutting Concerns

  • Transactions are not explicitly declared with @Transactional; metadata and storage operations are performed as separate steps.
  • Storage success followed by queue or metadata failure can leave the asset stored without complete processing or catalog metadata.
  • The application uses manual RabbitMQ acknowledgment, JSON message conversion, and durable queue declarations.
  • The backup profile listens to the processing queue for monitoring only. It requeues messages if acknowledgment handling fails.
  • Business-level authorization is not implemented in the reviewed controllers or services.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 2.7.18 and Java 8 are the central modernization constraints. Spring Boot 2.7 reached end-of-open-source-support status and should be migrated to a supported Boot and Java baseline. The AWS S3 SDK is explicitly managed as 2.25.13, while PostgreSQL, Jackson, Lombok, Thymeleaf, Spring Web, JPA, AMQP, and other Spring libraries are resolved through the Spring Boot parent BOM, so exact managed versions should be confirmed from a Maven dependency report or lock output before upgrade work.

Notable Observations

  • Spring AMQP, AWS SDK S3, Spring Data JPA, and the PostgreSQL driver are used across multiple modules and should be modeled as shared dependencies.
  • The web module contains all user-facing frameworks; the worker module relies on core Spring Boot, AMQP, JPA, AWS S3, and Jackson.
  • Lombok and Spring Boot DevTools are optional tooling dependencies rather than required application runtime services.
  • No Gradle lockfile or Maven lockfile is declared, so transitive dependency versions are not fixed in the repository build files.

Data Ownership Boundaries

The application uses one logical PostgreSQL database, assets_manager, shared by the web and worker modules rather than database-per-service isolation. Both modules contain the same JPA entity mapping and repository type, and both can read and write ImageMetadata. The web module creates metadata records for uploaded objects; the worker module updates records with thumbnail keys and URLs. Non-dev storage is S3, while dev storage is the local filesystem; file/object content is external to PostgreSQL, and only metadata is persisted there.

RabbitMQ is used for asynchronous image-processing handoff, but metadata access is coordinated through the shared database rather than a service API or dedicated cross-service aggregation query. Both modules perform full-table findAll() calls and then filter for matching keys, so the current read pattern is centralized and inefficient for large datasets. No CQRS or separate read/write models are implemented.
